common_name: Boreal Beast Honeyberry (University of Saskatchewan Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring alongside a compatible pollinizer such as Boreal Beauty or Boreal Blizzard; Boreal Beast is self-infertile and was released as part of the same University of Saskatchewan trio.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with at least one other overlapping-bloom haskap cultivar nearby, since Boreal Beast will not set fruit on its own. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program alongside Boreal Beauty and Boreal Blizzard, Boreal Beast is prized for its large, elongated fruit and vigorous, upright bush that holds its berries well without excessive drop as they ripen in mid-to-late season. Like other haskaps it tolerates winter cold to roughly -40F but struggles in hot, humid summer regions, making it best suited to short-season, cold-winter gardens. Avoid heavy pruning for the first three to four years beyond removing dead or crossing wood, since fruit forms on second-year and older growth, then begin light renewal pruning of the oldest canes to sustain production.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Wojtek blooms early and is commonly interplanted specifically as a pollinizer for cultivars like Aurora, Borealis, and Tundra rather than grown primarily for its own fruit.

directions: Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, spacing plants so their early flowers overlap with the bloom window of the main fruiting cultivars they are meant to pollinate. Wojtek is a Polish-bred haskap selection valued in North American plantings less for its own medium-sized, tangy berries than for its reliable early flowering, which makes it a favored cross-pollination partner for several popular Saskatchewan-bred honeyberry cultivars. The upright, vigorous bush is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter lows well below -30F, but performs poorly in hot, humid summer climates. Limit pruning in the first several years to dead or crossing wood, since haskaps fruit on second-year and older canes, then thin out the oldest stems periodically to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in warmer climates; prune to an open center to reduce mildew pressure.

directions: Plant dormant, thorny bushes in cool, fertile, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool and pruning to an open framework for good air movement and easier picking. Whitesmith is a long-established English dessert gooseberry prized for its smooth-skinned, pale greenish-white to creamy fruit that turns genuinely sweet once fully ripe, making it one of the better gooseberry cultivars for eating fresh rather than only cooking. The vigorous, slightly arching bush crops heavily but can be prone to mildew in humid conditions, so good spacing and airflow matter more than with some mildew-resistant modern hybrids. Harvest in stages, picking some berries green and firm for pies and preserves and leaving the rest to ripen fully for fresh eating.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

common_name: Lancashire Lad Gooseberry (Historic English Red Gooseberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; this vigorous old cultivar benefits from a sturdy support or open framework as the spreading branches fill with heavy fruit.

directions: Plant in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in a spot with some afternoon shade in warmer regions, and prune annually to an open shape since this is a naturally spreading, thorny bush. Lancashire Lad is a 19th-century English heirloom once among the most popular cultivars grown for the competitive gooseberry-showing clubs of Lancashire and Cheshire, prized for its large size as much as its flavor. The fruit is downy-skinned and dark red at maturity, tart enough for excellent cooking and preserving when picked slightly underripe, and mellowing to a richer flavor if left to fully color on the bush. Its heavy cropping and cold hardiness have kept it in cultivation among heirloom fruit collectors long after most Victorian-era show cultivars faded from commerce.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Erntesegen is self-fertile and, like other lingonberry cultivars, typically produces a lighter summer crop followed by a heavier fall crop.

directions: Grow in partial shade to full sun in very acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, the same conditions favored by blueberries and other ericaceous shrubs. Erntesegen, German for 'harvest blessing', is a long-established European lingonberry cultivar bred specifically for unusually heavy, dependable fruit set, producing abundant clusters of small, tart, bright-red berries on a dense, low, evergreen mat. Its glossy foliage doubles as an attractive year-round groundcover, and its shade tolerance relative to most fruiting shrubs makes it a good underplanting for blueberries or acid-loving conifers. Shear plantings back lightly every few years to renew growth and keep the mat dense and productive, and harvest the fall crop after the berries deepen to full red for the best flavor.

common_name: Eastham Beach Plum (Named Cape Cod Beach Plum Selection)

planting.note: Plant in sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in spring alongside a second beach plum cultivar such as Squibnocket or Hancock for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in sandy, salt-spray-exposed, well-drained soil in full sun, siting near another named beach plum cultivar since seedlings and single clones set fruit poorly on their own. Eastham is one of the older Massachusetts-selected beach plum cultivars, chosen for large, well-flavored fruit and heavy, dependable cropping compared with typical wild seedling stands. Its purple-red fruit is prized for jams, jellies, and the traditional New England beach plum preserves that built the species' local reputation. Being a true coastal native, it tolerates salt spray, drought, and lean sandy soil that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, making it as useful for dune stabilization as for harvest. Prune lightly after flowering only to remove dead or crossing wood, since heavy pruning reduces the following year's crop.
